title: Green wood: seasoning and storage
subtitle: How to dry green wood billets without checking, and how to store them for later use
excerpt: Green wood that dries too fast or unevenly checks, splits along the grain from internal stress. Knowing how to slow the drying in cut billets, when to end-seal, how to stack for air circulation, and how long each species takes to season for different projects is the difference between usable timber and a pile of checked waste.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the seasoning method; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the species-specific drying times and end-sealing guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled wood, still high in moisture content. Green wood carves easily but must be managed carefully during drying.
Surface splits that form in wood as it dries unevenly. End-grain dries faster than side grain, which causes tension that splits along the grain.
A short section of split or round timber, the working unit in green woodwork.
Coating the cut ends of a billet with wax, PVA, or green wood bark to slow moisture loss at the end-grain and reduce checking.

content.text: Fresh
green wood
dries from the outside in. The outer surfaces lose moisture faster than the core, which causes the outer layers to shrink against a still-moist core. This tension splits the wood along the grain,
checking
. The end-grain dries ten to twelve times faster than the side grain, so end-checking is always more severe than side-checking. Managing the drying rate is the skill.
Which billets need managing
Round billets (log sections) are the highest risk, drying happens from all surfaces simultaneously and end-checking is severe.
Riven billets (split sections) are lower risk because the split faces dry at similar rates.
End-sealing
is still worth doing on high-value billets.
Small billets under 3 cm diameter or thin sections dry too fast to control, use these within a week of cutting or keep in water.
End-sealing
Coat the cut ends of a
billet
within an hour of cutting. Options in order of effectiveness:
Candle wax or household paraffin wax: melt and paint on with a brush. Seals for months.
Thick PVA glue: paint on and let dry. Effective for a few weeks and re-applicable.

Bark left on: if the billet still has its bark on the side, leave it. The bark acts as a natural moisture barrier on the side grain. Do not strip bark until the billet has been worked or has seasoned completely.
Stacking for air drying

Stack billets with spacers (stickers) between each layer so air circulates on all faces. The stack should be under cover, roof overhead, sides open, in a location with constant gentle airflow. An indoor shed or garage is slightly too warm and still for the first few months; a covered outdoor lean-to is better. Avoid full sun on freshly cut billets, the temperature differential on the exposed face causes checking within hours.
Keeping billets in water

Small billets can be stored submerged in a bucket of water for one to two weeks without any loss of working quality. Change the water weekly. This method works for spoon billets, rod sections, and small kuksa blanks. Not practical for larger sections or winter conditions.
Seasoning times by species and use
Hazel rod, 3 cm diameter, spoon use: 6, 8 weeks under cover.
Birch billet, 10 cm diameter, kuksa blank: 3, 4 months minimum; check regularly for surface checking.
Ash, 8 cm diameter, for tool handles or chair components: 6, 12 months, allowing one year per 2.5 cm of thickness as a rough rule.
Lime, 15 cm section, for carving blocks: 12, 18 months. Lime checks severely if rushed.
Carve green, dry slowly

The best approach for carved pieces, spoons, kuksa, faces, is to carve them while green, then dry them slowly. Carving removes the outer layers and reduces the section thickness; a 10 mm wall dries in weeks without checking, whereas the original 50 mm billet would take months and still check. Carve the piece close to final form while the wood is green, then end-seal the tip and handle end and lay it on a shelf under cover. Check weekly for checking; if surface cracks appear, wrap the piece loosely in cloth for slower drying.
